Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: The Same But Different: Structural Similarities and Differences in Multilingual Language Modeling
papers.research_question: When two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? When two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs use shared internal circuitry for similar syntactic processes across languages, even in independently trained monolingual models, and employ language-specific components (e.g., feed-forward networks) for language-specific morphological processes.
papers.conclusion: The paper finds that cross-lingual structural similarity is represented within LLMs using shared circuits that invoke the same algorithm independent of language, and that language-specific processing is localized to play a causal role only in languages that require it.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual models use a single circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs.
Monolingual models trained independently on English and Chinese each adopt nearly the same circuit for the IOI task, suggesting consistency in how LLMs learn to handle this aspect of language modeling.
For tasks requiring language-specific morphological processes (e.g., past tense marking in English), multilingual models invoke a largely overlapping circuit but employ language-specific components as needed, such as feed-forward networks in English only for morphological marking.
The circuits identified for the IOI task align with prior work, indicating that the same mechanism is shared between English and Chinese within a multilingual model.
Heads specifically responsible for past tense disambiguation are activated in English but not in Chinese, and they suppress present-tense verbs in English.
papers.limitation: Results are limited to specific tasks and datasets, requiring future work for replication and generalization.
future_direction: Replicate and generalize findings to more tasks and datasets.
Explore cross-disciplinary collaborations to gain fresh perspectives on linguistic universality using LLMs.
Investigate whether circuit overlap can be exploited for improving cross-lingual transfer and safety.
papers.abstract: We employ new tools from mechanistic interpretability in order to ask whether the internal structure of large language models (LLMs) shows correspondence to the linguistic structures which underlie the languages on which they are trained. In particular, we ask (1) when two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? and (2) when two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry? Using English and Chinese multilingual and monolingual models, we analyze the internal circuitry involved in two tasks. We find evidence that models employ the same circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs, and that this is the case even for monolingual models trained completely independently. Moreover, we show that multilingual models employ language-specific components (attention heads and feed-forward networks) when needed to handle linguistic processes (e.g., morphological marking) that only exist in some languages. Together, our results provide new insights into how LLMs trade off between exploiting common structures and preserving linguistic differences when tasked with modeling multiple languages simultaneously.

papers.title: Conceptual structure coheres in human cognition but not in large language models
papers.research_question: Does conceptual structure in large language models cohere across different probing tasks as it does in humans, or do human and LLM conceptual representations differ in robustness?
papers.core_contribution: Human conceptual structure is robust across different tasks and cultures, but large language models exhibit less coherence in conceptual structure across different probing tasks, indicating a lack of a stable conceptual core.
papers.conclusion: Human conceptual structure is robust to differences in task, language, and culture, while contemporary LLMs lack such coherence, highlighting a fundamental difference between human cognition and current machine language models.
papers.key_findings:
Human conceptual structure estimates from three different tasks (feature listing, triadic comparisons, pairwise ratings) are highly coherent (squared Procrustes correlations between 0.72 and 0.96).
LLM conceptual structure estimates vary depending on the probing task; for GPT-3, the squared Procrustes correlations between different task embeddings are lower (e.g., 0.72 between feature listing and triplet, 0.47 between feature listing and pairwise, 0.25 between triplet and pairwise).
LLM conceptual structure from verified feature lists aligns moderately well with human feature norms (squared Procrustes correlation 0.89), but other LLM-derived embeddings align less well.
Chain-of-thought prompting improves alignment with human conceptual structure for some models but does not achieve human-level coherence.
Embeddings from internal representations (e.g., GPT-3 hidden layers, word2vec, CLIP) do not cohere well with each other or with human embeddings.
papers.limitation:
The study uses a constrained set of 30 concepts from two domains; a larger scale study might reveal different results.
The LLM simulations did not employ advanced prompting techniques like tree-of-thought or self-consistency, which might improve coherence.
LLMs lack multimodal sensory experience that humans have, which might affect conceptual organization.
future_direction: Conduct a larger scale study on larger concept sets.
Investigate the use of advanced prompting techniques (e.g., tree-of-thought, self-consistency) to improve conceptual coherence in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Neural network models of language have long been used as a tool for developing hypotheses about conceptual representation in the mind and brain. For many years, such use involved extracting vector-space representations of words and using distances among these to predict or understand human behavior in various semantic tasks. Contemporary large language models (LLMs), however, make it possible to interrogate the latent structure of conceptual representations using experimental methods nearly identical to those commonly used with human participants. The current work utilizes three common techniques borrowed from cognitive psychology to estimate and compare the structure of concepts in humans and a suite of LLMs. In humans, we show that conceptual structure is robust to differences in culture, language, and method of estimation. Structures estimated from LLM behavior, while individually fairly consistent with those estimated from human behavior, vary much more depending upon the particular task used to generate responses--across tasks, estimates of conceptual structure from the very same model cohere less with one another than do human structure estimates. These results highlight an important difference between contemporary LLMs and human cognition, with implications for understanding some fundamental limitations of contemporary machine language.

papers.title: Unveiling Factual Recall Behaviors of Large Language Models through Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How effectively do Large Language Models retrieve and utilize their internal factual knowledge for multi-hop reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs often fail to retrieve relevant factual knowledge during reasoning; enhancing factual recall improves reasoning performance, while Chain-of-Thought prompting helps by stimulating step-by-step reasoning and reducing shortcuts.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall is crucial for correct reasoning in LLMs; CoT stimulates recall and reduces shortcuts, and contextual conflicts can affect the retrieval process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not consistently retrieve pertinent factual knowledge for reasoning, with more than a third of reasoning errors stemming from deficiencies in retrieval.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting enhances factual recall by facilitating step-by-step reasoning, reducing the likelihood of shortcuts.
Manually enhancing the factual recall process improves reasoning performance, while suppressing it leads to notable degradation.
The presence of knowledge conflict in the context can enhance the retrieval of the corresponding fact during reasoning.
A considerable proportion of correctly answered questions under no CoT setting rely on shortcuts rather than full multi-hop reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability: Findings are based on specific LLMs and the TFRKN dataset; future research should extend to various models and datasets.
Theoretical Analysis: Empirical evidence is provided, but a deeper theoretical analysis is needed to fully comprehend the underlying reasons.
Practical Applications: The paper discusses theoretical aspects but does not delve into practical applications to enhance reasoning capabilities.
future_direction: Extend findings to verify generalizability across various models and datasets.
Conduct deeper theoretical analysis to understand the observed phenomena.
Explore how the findings can be applied in practical scenarios to enhance LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) actively recall or retrieve their internal repositories of factual knowledge when faced with reasoning tasks. Through an analysis of LLMs' internal factual recall at each reasoning step via Knowledge Neurons, we reveal that LLMs fail to harness the critical factual associations under certain circumstances. Instead, they tend to opt for alternative, shortcut-like pathways to answer reasoning questions. By manually manipulating the recall process of parametric knowledge in LLMs, we demonstrate that enhancing this recall process directly improves reasoning performance whereas suppressing it leads to notable degradation. Furthermore, we assess the effect of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a powerful technique for addressing complex reasoning tasks. Our findings indicate that CoT can intensify the recall of factual knowledge by encouraging LLMs to engage in orderly and reliable reasoning. Furthermore, we explored how contextual conflicts affect the retrieval of facts during the reasoning process to gain a comprehensive understanding of the factual recall behaviors of LLMs. Code and data will be available soon.

papers.title: Towards Revealing the Mystery behind Chain of Thought: A Theoretical Perspective
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms behind Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and how does it unlock the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) for mathematical and reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper theoretically proves that bounded-depth Transformers without Chain-of-Thought (CoT) require super-polynomial size to solve basic mathematical tasks, while constant-size autoregressive Transformers with CoT can solve them, and extends this to show CoT enables solving dynamic programming problems.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-Thought is the key to unlocking the reasoning capabilities of autoregressive Transformers, both theoretically and empirically, by allowing step-by-step generation that overcomes the expressivity limitations of bounded-depth models.
papers.key_findings:
Bounded-depth log-precision Transformers of polynomial size cannot directly solve arithmetic and linear equation tasks unless the model size grows super-polynomially with input length.
Autoregressive Transformers of constant depth and size can generate correct CoT solutions for arithmetic and linear equation tasks.
LLMs with CoT can solve a general class of decision-making problems formulated as dynamic programming.
Experimental results show Transformers fail to directly predict answers but consistently learn to generate correct step-by-step CoT solutions given sufficient demonstrations.
CoT increases the effective depth of the Transformer circuit, allowing it to solve problems beyond the TC0 complexity class.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have discovered that Chain-of-Thought prompting (CoT) can dramatically improve the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs), particularly when dealing with complex tasks involving mathematics or reasoning. Despite the enormous empirical success, the underlying mechanisms behind CoT and how it unlocks the potential of LLMs remain elusive. In this paper, we take a first step towards theoretically answering these questions. Specifically, we examine the expressivity of LLMs with CoT in solving fundamental mathematical and decision-making problems. By using circuit complexity theory, we first give impossibility results showing that bounded-depth Transformers are unable to directly produce correct answers for basic arithmetic/equation tasks unless the model size grows super-polynomially with respect to the input length. In contrast, we then prove by construction that autoregressive Transformers of constant size suffice to solve both tasks by generating CoT derivations using a commonly used math language format. Moreover, we show LLMs with CoT can handle a general class of decision-making problems known as Dynamic Programming, thus justifying its power in tackling complex real-world tasks. Finally, an extensive set of experiments show that, while Transformers always fail to directly predict the answers, they can consistently learn to generate correct solutions step-by-step given sufficient CoT demonstrations.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of Morphological Content in BERT Models for Multiple Languages
papers.research_question: To what extent do BERT-style models encode morphological feature information in their hidden representations and attention distributions for multiple languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that BERT-style models encode morphological information by partitioning their embedding space into convex regions correlated with feature values, that contextualized embeddings help disambiguate ambiguous forms but not completely, and that specific attention head/layer combinations focus on subject-verb agreement.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that pre-trained BERT-style models are sensitive to morphological information, with strong performance on feature-value classification and certain attention heads learning to focus attention in a manner consistent with morphological agreement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-style models partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value.
Contextualized embeddings allow models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases.
Specific attention head/layer combinations hone in on subject-verb agreement.
Supervision significantly aids in extracting morphological information, as unsupervised clustering performs near random baselines.
Morphological information is best represented in the middle layers for languages with complex morphology (German and Russian), while for simpler languages it is present throughout all layers.
papers.limitation:
Models have difficulty disambiguating syncretic (ambiguous) forms, especially in languages with complex inflectional morphology.
The classification tasks require supervision; unsupervised methods (k-means) perform near random baselines.
future_direction: Identifying morphological information in BERT-style models in an unsupervised fashion.
Improving models' ability to disambiguate syncretic forms for languages with complex inflectional morphology.
Further exploration of how morphological information is shared between words via self-attention.
papers.abstract: This work describes experiments which probe the hidden representations of several BERT-style models for morphological content. The goal is to examine the extent to which discrete linguistic structure, in the form of morphological features and feature values, presents itself in the vector representations and attention distributions of pre-trained language models for five European languages. The experiments contained herein show that (i) Transformer architectures largely partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value, (ii) the contextualized nature of transformer embeddings allows models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases, and (iii) very specific attention head/layer combinations appear to hone in on subject-verb agreement.

papers.title: Reasoning with Latent Thoughts: On the Power of Looped Transformers
papers.research_question: Does reasoning require large depth but not necessarily many parameters, and can looped models effectively solve reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Looped transformers can solve reasoning tasks with fewer parameters by providing depth through looping, and they exhibit an inductive bias towards reasoning over memorization.
papers.conclusion: Looped models are effective for reasoning tasks, providing depth without many parameters, and have an inductive bias towards improving reasoning performance over memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Looped models nearly match the performance of non-looped models with the same depth on synthetic reasoning tasks like addition, p-hop induction, and i-GSM, despite having fewer parameters.
For language modeling, looped models have worse perplexity but better reasoning performance on downstream tasks compared to non-looped models with the same FLOPs.
Looped models show scaling behavior with effective depth similar to chain-of-thought reasoning.
Theoretically, looped models can simulate iterative algorithms and chain-of-thought reasoning.
A regularization method that encourages layer similarity inherits the inductive bias of looped models towards reasoning.
papers.limitation: The results are limited to the tested reasoning problems and may not generalize to other forms of reasoning (e.g., multimodal and common-sense reasoning).
future_direction: Generalizing the results to other forms of reasoning such as multimodal and common-sense reasoning.
Formalizing reasoning problems more succinctly.
Further exploration of the inductive bias towards reasoning at the same perplexity.
papers.abstract: Large language models have shown remarkable reasoning abilities and scaling laws suggest that large parameter count, especially along the depth axis, is the primary driver. In this work, we make a stronger claim -- many reasoning problems require a large depth but not necessarily many parameters. This unlocks a novel application of looped models for reasoning. Firstly, we show that for many synthetic reasoning problems like addition, $p$-hop induction, and math problems, a $k$-layer transformer looped $L$ times nearly matches the performance of a $kL$-layer non-looped model, and is significantly better than a $k$-layer model. This is further corroborated by theoretical results showing that many such reasoning problems can be solved via iterative algorithms, and thus, can be solved effectively using looped models with nearly optimal depth. Perhaps surprisingly, these benefits also translate to practical settings of language modeling -- on many downstream reasoning tasks, a language model with $k$-layers looped $L$ times can be competitive to, if not better than, a $kL$-layer language model. In fact, our empirical analysis reveals an intriguing phenomenon: looped and non-looped models exhibit scaling behavior that depends on their effective depth, akin to the inference-time scaling of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. We further elucidate the connection to CoT reasoning by proving that looped models implicitly generate latent thoughts and can simulate $T$ steps of CoT with $T$ loops. Inspired by these findings, we also present an interesting dichotomy between reasoning and memorization, and design a looping-based regularization that is effective on both fronts.

papers.title: Schoenfeld's Anatomy of Mathematical Reasoning by Language Models
papers.research_question: Do reasoning traces exhibit consistent structure when abstracted into functional episodes? How do reasoning dynamics differ across models? How do episode patterns correlate with correctness and efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ThinkARM, a framework for abstracting reasoning traces into functional episodes, enabling systematic analysis of reasoning structure and dynamics in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Episode-level representations make reasoning steps explicit, enabling systematic analysis of how reasoning is structured, stabilized, and altered in modern language models.
papers.key_findings:
Episode-level analysis reveals a functional progression from abstract reasoning to concrete execution to evaluative control.
Reasoning models distribute effort across analysis, exploration, execution, and verification, while non-reasoning models are heavily execution-focused.
Exploration serves as a critical branching point: correct solutions route exploration into monitoring or re-analysis, while incorrect ones tend to continue execution or terminate.
Efficient reasoning methods selectively suppress evaluation-oriented episodes and feedback loops, diverging from base model patterns.
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly expose reasoning traces, yet their underlying cognitive structure and steps remain difficult to identify and analyze beyond surface-level statistics. We adopt Schoenfeld's Episode Theory as an inductive, intermediate-scale lens and introduce ThinkARM (Anatomy of Reasoning in Models), a scalable framework that explicitly abstracts reasoning traces into functional reasoning steps such as Analysis, Explore, Implement, Verify, etc. When applied to mathematical problem solving by diverse models, this abstraction reveals reproducible thinking dynamics and structural differences between reasoning and non-reasoning models, which are not apparent from token-level views. We further present two diagnostic case studies showing that exploration functions as a critical branching step associated with correctness, and that efficiency-oriented methods selectively suppress evaluative feedback steps rather than uniformly shortening responses. Together, our results demonstrate that episode-level representations make reasoning steps explicit, enabling systematic analysis of how reasoning is structured, stabilized, and altered in modern language models.

papers.title: Probing for the Usage of Grammatical Number
papers.research_question: How does BERT encode grammatical number, and does it actually use that encoding when solving the number agreement task?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a usage-based probing setup to find functional encodings, and shows that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number for number agreement, with separate encodings for nouns and verbs, and identifies transfer layers.
papers.conclusion: The usage-based probing method allows tracking how grammatical number is encoded and transferred in BERT, showing that interventions impact behavior and extractability, revealing orthogonal encodings for nouns and verbs, and indirect transfer through intermediate tokens.
papers.key_findings:
BERT relies on a linear functional encoding of grammatical number to solve the number agreement task.
BERT uses separate encodings of grammatical number for nouns and verbs.
Number information is transferred from noun to verb between layers 3 and 8.
The transfer occurs indirectly through intermediate tokens, not directly via attention.
The encoding found by diagnostic probes is actually used by the model (functional).
papers.limitation:
The dataset may not be fully representative of the number agreement task.
Amnesic probing may remove more information than necessary.
papers.abstract: A central quest of probing is to uncover how pre-trained models encode a linguistic property within their representations. An encoding, however, might be spurious-i.e., the model might not rely on it when making predictions. In this paper, we try to find an encoding that the model actually uses, introducing a usage-based probing setup. We first choose a behavioral task which cannot be solved without using the linguistic property. Then, we attempt to remove the property by intervening on the model's representations. We contend that, if an encoding is used by the model, its removal should harm the performance on the chosen behavioral task. As a case study, we focus on how BERT encodes grammatical number, and on how it uses this encoding to solve the number agreement task. Experimentally, we find that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number to produce the correct behavioral output. We also find that BERT uses a separate encoding of grammatical number for nouns and verbs. Finally, we identify in which layers information about grammatical number is transferred from a noun to its head verb.

papers.title: Scaling Competence, Shrinking Reasoning: Cognitive Signatures in Language Model Learning
papers.research_question: How do reasoning tokens evolve during fine-tuning, and can they serve as indicators of learning stages?
papers.core_contribution: Reasoning tokens in language models expand, peak, and contract during fine-tuning, mirroring the Four Stages of Competence, and their dynamics can serve as metrics for diagnosing training stages and guiding early stopping.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning tokens serve as a dynamic scaffold during fine-tuning, providing insights into model learning dynamics and practical tools for diagnosing training progress and optimizing learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning token length increases with performance early in training, peaks at conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task.
Models retain task performance after training even when reasoning tokens are removed, indicating that reasoning scaffolds learning but becomes unnecessary once competence is acquired.
The progression of reasoning tokens aligns with the Four Stages of Competence framework from cognitive science.
Reasoning token dynamics can diagnose training stages, detect convergence, and inform early stopping criteria.
The pattern is consistent across multiple models and tasks including code generation, math problems, and logical question answering.
papers.limitation:
Reasoning token length and correctness are surface-level proxies for internal cognitive processes, and the use of competence stages is interpretive rather than diagnostic.
Experiments are limited to math, logic, and code generation tasks, and may not generalize to tasks with high ambiguity or contextual sensitivity.
The proposed metrics may be less stable in settings with noisy supervision, curriculum learning, or large-scale instruction tuning.
future_direction: Future work may formalize these analogies further or challenge them with deeper mechanistic analysis.
papers.abstract: We analyze reasoning in language models during task-specific fine-tuning and draws parallel between reasoning tokens--intermediate steps generated while solving problem and the human working memory. Drawing from cognitive science, we align training dynamics with the Four Stages of Competence: models initially produce incorrect outputs without reasoning, then begin reasoning (but still fail), eventually reason effectively, and finally solve tasks without explicit reasoning. We find that reasoning token length expands as performance improves, peaks at the stage of conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task. Notably, after training, models retain performance even when reasoning is removed--suggesting it scaffolded learning but is no longer needed. This progression offers actionable insights: reasoning token dynamics can serve as a signal for diagnosing training stage, identifying convergence, and guiding early stopping. We propose metrics to track this trajectory and argue that reasoning behavior is valuable for understanding and optimizing reasoning model training.

papers.title: Temporal Predictors of Outcome in Reasoning Language Models
papers.abstract: The chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigm uses the elicitation of step-by-step rationales as a proxy for reasoning, gradually refining the model's latent representation of a solution. However, it remains unclear just how early a Large Language Model (LLM) internally commits to an eventual outcome. We probe this by training linear classifiers on hidden states after the first t reasoning tokens, showing that eventual correctness is highly predictable after only a few tokens, even when longer outputs are needed to reach a definite answer. We show that, for harder questions, a drop in predictive accuracy highlights a selection artifact: hard items are disproportionately represented in long CoTs. Overall, our results imply that for reasoning models, internal self-assessment of success tends to emerge after only a few tokens, with implications for interpretability and for inference-time control.

papers.title: Analyzing LLMs' Knowledge Boundary Cognition Across Languages Through the Lens of Internal Representations
papers.research_question: How do LLMs recognize knowledge boundaries across different languages, and can this ability be transferred or enhanced?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes how LLMs perceive knowledge boundaries across languages, finds that this perception is encoded in middle layers with linear structure, and proposes training-free alignment and fine-tuning methods to transfer and enhance this ability.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that LLMs encode knowledge boundary cognition in middle layers with linear structure, enabling cross-lingual transfer through training-free alignment and fine-tuning, providing insights and methods for improving hallucination reduction in low-resource languages.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge boundary cognition is encoded in the middle to middle-upper layers of LLMs across languages.
Language differences in knowledge boundary perception follow a linear structure, enabling training-free alignment methods like mean-shifting and linear projection.
Training-free methods effectively transfer knowledge boundary perception across languages, reducing the performance gap.
Fine-tuning on bilingual question translation data enhances LLMs' recognition of knowledge boundaries across languages.
A weak-to-strong generalization pattern where probes trained on low-resource languages perform better on projected high-resource representations.
papers.limitation: It is difficult to investigate how representations evolve during the generation process, such as in chain-of-thought reasoning, due to challenges in locating when transformations occur.
future_direction: Investigating how knowledge boundary representations evolve during the generation process, especially in long chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.abstract: While understanding the knowledge boundaries of LLMs is crucial to prevent hallucination, research on the knowledge boundaries of LLMs has predominantly focused on English. In this work, we present the first study to analyze how LLMs recognize knowledge boundaries across different languages by probing their internal representations when processing known and unknown questions in multiple languages. Our empirical studies reveal three key findings: 1) LLMs' perceptions of knowledge boundaries are encoded in the middle to middle-upper layers across different languages. 2) Language differences in knowledge boundary perception follow a linear structure, which motivates our proposal of a training-free alignment method that effectively transfers knowledge boundary perception ability across languages, thereby helping reduce hallucination risk in low-resource languages; 3) Fine-tuning on bilingual question pair translation further enhances LLMs' recognition of knowledge boundaries across languages. Given the absence of standard testbeds for cross-lingual knowledge boundary analysis, we construct a multilingual evaluation suite comprising three representative types of knowledge boundary data. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/DAMO-NLP-SG/LLM-Multilingual-Knowledge-Boundaries.

papers.title: On the Representational Capacity of Neural Language Models with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the representational capacity of neural language models (LMs) when augmented with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning? Specifically, can CoT-augmented LMs represent the same family of distributions over strings as probabilistic Turing machines?
papers.core_contribution: This paper formalizes chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in a probabilistic setting and shows that recurrent and transformer language models augmented with CoT reasoning can represent the same family of distributions over strings as probabilistic Turing machines.
papers.conclusion: CoT reasoning increases the computational power of neural language models by allowing them to perform additional sequential computation and keep track of execution trajectories, effectively introducing non-determinism and enabling simulation of probabilistic Turing machines.
papers.key_findings:
CoT-augmented constant-precision RNN LMs are equivalent to probabilistic finite-state automata (PFSAs), whereas without CoT they are equivalent to deterministic PFSAs.
CoT-augmented RNN LMs with linearly bounded precision and transformer LMs with logarithmically bounded precision can simulate any probabilistic Turing machine.
CoT reasoning provides a principled way to overcome the limitation of deterministic computation in fixed-precision neural models, allowing them to simulate non-deterministic automata.

papers.title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint
papers.research_question: How do transformers balance global knowledge and in-context learning during training, specifically in the development of induction head mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic bigram dataset and an associative memory viewpoint to study learning dynamics in two-layer transformers, showing that induction heads emerge through top-down gradient-based learning.
papers.conclusion: The associative memory viewpoint provides valuable insights into transformer learning dynamics, offering a foundation for better interpretability and improvements in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Global bigram associations are learned rapidly, while in-context induction mechanisms develop more slowly.
Transformer weight matrices can be viewed as associative memories that store input-output embedding pairs.
The induction head mechanism forms in a top-down manner, with output matrices learning before key-query matrices.
Theoretical gradient analysis shows how associative memories are recovered from noisy inputs during training.
Data distribution properties, such as trigger frequency and output uniformity, affect the learning speed and accuracy of associative memories.
papers.limitation:
The simplified transformer architecture lacks components like non-linear MLPs, multiple heads, and layer normalization, which are present in standard transformers.
The synthetic dataset may not fully capture the complexity of real-world language data.
future_direction: Extending the associative memory viewpoint to non-linear components and multi-head architectures.
Applying insights to optimization algorithms, data selection, and model editing for LLMs.
Studying how such mechanisms scale to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models based on transformers have achieved great empirical successes. However, as they are deployed more widely, there is a growing need to better understand their internal mechanisms in order to make them more reliable. These models appear to store vast amounts of knowledge from their training data, and to adapt quickly to new information provided in their context or prompt. We study how transformers balance these two types of knowledge by considering a synthetic setup where tokens are generated from either global or context-specific bigram distributions. By a careful empirical analysis of the training process on a simplified two-layer transformer, we illustrate the fast learning of global bigrams and the slower development of an "induction head" mechanism for the in-context bigrams. We highlight the role of weight matrices as associative memories, provide theoretical insights on how gradients enable their learning during training, and study the role of data-distributional properties.

papers.title: Demystifying Reasoning Dynamics with Mutual Information: Thinking Tokens are Information Peaks in LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What are the critical reasoning steps or intermediate states that significantly affect the final results in the reasoning process of large reasoning models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that during the reasoning process of large reasoning models (LRMs), certain steps exhibit sudden increases in mutual information (MI) with the correct answer, and these MI peaks correspond to 'thinking tokens' (e.g., 'Hmm', 'Wait') that are critical for reasoning performance. Based on this, the paper proposes two training-free methods to improve reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that thinking tokens, which correspond to MI peaks, are crucial for LRM reasoning and that leveraging these tokens can improve reasoning performance without additional training.
papers.key_findings:
During LRM reasoning, certain steps show sudden and significant increases in mutual information (MI) with the golden answer, termed MI peaks.
The tokens at MI peaks are often reflective or transitional words (e.g., 'Hmm', 'Wait', 'So') and are critical for reasoning performance; suppressing them significantly harms performance.
Theoretically, higher cumulative MI between representations and the golden answer leads to tighter bounds on prediction error.
Non-reasoning LLMs do not exhibit clear MI peaks, suggesting the phenomenon is a result of reasoning-intensive training.
Two proposed methods, Representation Recycling (RR) and Thinking Token based Test-time Scaling (TTTS), which leverage thinking tokens, can improve reasoning performance on math benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in complex problem-solving, yet their internal reasoning mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the reasoning trajectories of LRMs from an information-theoretic perspective. By tracking how mutual information (MI) between intermediate representations and the correct answer evolves during LRM reasoning, we observe an interesting MI peaks phenomenon: the MI at specific generative steps exhibits a sudden and significant increase during LRM's reasoning process. We theoretically analyze such phenomenon and show that as MI increases, the probability of model's prediction error decreases. Furthermore, these MI peaks often correspond to tokens expressing reflection or transition, such as ``Hmm'', ``Wait'' and ``Therefore,'' which we term as the thinking tokens. We then demonstrate that these thinking tokens are crucial for LRM's reasoning performance, while other tokens has minimal impacts. Building on these analyses, we propose two simple yet effective methods to improve LRM's reasoning performance, by delicately leveraging these thinking tokens. Overall, our work provides novel insights into the reasoning mechanisms of LRMs and offers practical ways to improve their reasoning capabilities. The code is available at https://github.com/ChnQ/MI-Peaks.

papers.title: Emergent World Representations: Exploring a Sequence Model Trained on a Synthetic Task
papers.research_question: Does a sequence model trained on a synthetic task (Othello game transcripts) learn an internal representation of the board state, and is that representation causal to its predictions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that a GPT model trained on Othello game transcripts learns a nonlinear internal representation of the board state, which is causally involved in its predictions. It introduces intervention techniques and latent saliency maps for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The experiments provide evidence that Othello-GPT maintains a nonlinear internal representation of the game board state, which is causally linked to its predictions. The tools introduced (nonlinear probes, interventions, latent saliency maps) may prove useful for interpretability in natural language settings.
papers.key_findings:
Othello-GPT predicts legal moves with high accuracy, and this is not due to memorization.
Nonlinear probes can accurately decode the board state from internal activations, while linear probes perform poorly.
Intervention experiments show that the board representation is causal to the model's predictions.
Latent saliency maps reveal differences between models trained on synthetic vs. championship data, indicating different learned strategies.
The internal representation of the board state is nonlinear and emerges during training.
papers.limitation: Latent saliency maps only attribute to one tile when multiple tiles are involved in a move, which does not fully capture the Othello rule logic.
future_direction: Extend investigation to other, more complex games.
Compare strategies learned by a sequence model with those of a model trained with a priori knowledge of Othello.
Study how results generalize to natural language models.
papers.abstract: Language models show a surprising range of capabilities, but the source of their apparent competence is unclear. Do these networks just memorize a collection of surface statistics, or do they rely on internal representations of the process that generates the sequences they see? We investigate this question by applying a variant of the GPT model to the task of predicting legal moves in a simple board game, Othello. Although the network has no a priori knowledge of the game or its rules, we uncover evidence of an emergent nonlinear internal representation of the board state. Interventional experiments indicate this representation can be used to control the output of the network and create "latent saliency maps" that can help explain predictions in human terms.

papers.title: Language Models Are Greedy Reasoners: A Systematic Formal Analysis of Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: To what extent do large language models (LLMs) reason via chain-of-thought prompting, and do they rely on simple heuristics rather than genuine reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the PRONTO QA dataset and uses formal analysis to show that LLMs are capable of correct individual deduction steps but struggle with proof planning when multiple valid steps are available.
papers.conclusion: While the largest LLMs are generally capable of reasoning, they have difficulty with proof planning and selecting the correct proof step when multiple options are available.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are capable of making valid individual proof steps, even in fictional contexts.
LLMs have difficulty with proof planning: when multiple valid proof steps are available, they often select the wrong step, leading to incomplete proofs.
Real-world knowledge helps reasoning: performance is significantly better with true ontologies compared to fictional or false ones.
Longer proofs (5 hops) are challenging, especially with top-down traversal of the ontology.
For larger models, the main source of error is misleading steps rather than invalid steps.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to modus ponens, proof lengths of at most 5, and semantically simple sentences.
future_direction: Use PRONTO QA to compare LLM reasoning with human reasoning and explore which aspects of human reasoning LLMs acquired.
Develop reasoning systems with more sophisticated proof planning/search strategies, such as neurosymbolic approaches.
Investigate whether LLMs can produce longer proofs, reason with other deduction rules, or handle more semantically complex sentences.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable reasoning capabilities given chain-of-thought prompts (examples with intermediate reasoning steps). Existing benchmarks measure reasoning ability indirectly, by evaluating accuracy on downstream tasks such as mathematical reasoning. However, it is unclear how these models obtain the answers and whether they rely on simple heuristics rather than the generated chain-of-thought. To enable systematic exploration of the reasoning ability of LLMs, we present a new synthetic question-answering dataset called PrOntoQA, where each example is generated from a synthetic world model represented in first-order logic. This allows us to parse the generated chain-of-thought into symbolic proofs for formal analysis. Our analysis on InstructGPT and GPT-3 shows that LLMs are quite capable of making correct individual deduction steps, and so are generally capable of reasoning, even in fictional contexts. However, they have difficulty with proof planning: When multiple valid deduction steps are available, they are not able to systematically explore the different options.

papers.title: On the Sub-layer Functionalities of Transformer Decoder
papers.research_question: How do source and target information evolve within the Transformer decoder layer-by-layer and module-by-module? How does the Source Exploitation Module (SEM) exploit source information in different layers? How does the Information Fusion Module (IFM) fuse source and target information?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes the functionalities of sub-layers within the Transformer decoder for neural machine translation, introducing a universal probing scheme. A key finding is that the residual feed-forward module can be removed with minimal performance loss, significantly boosting speed.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into how the Transformer decoder leverages source and target information across layers and modules. These findings can inspire architectural improvements, such as incorporating external alignment signals, exploring different sub-layer stacking orders, and pruning redundant components for efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
The Source Exploitation Module (SEM) guides the representation evolution of both source and target information within the decoder.
Higher-layer SEMs focus on word alignment, while lower-layer SEMs gather broader source context.
The Target Exploitation Module (TEM) is critical for building word alignments in SEM, but its stacking order with SEM is not essential.
The Information Fusion Module (IFM) can be simplified to a single Add&Norm operation, removing the feed-forward network, with minimal translation quality loss and significant speed improvements.
The simplified decoder (without feed-forward modules) achieves comparable BLEU scores while increasing training and inference speed by 11-14% for Base models and up to 50% for inference on some tasks.
future_direction: Improving word alignment of higher SEMs by incorporating external alignment signals.
Exploring the stacking order of SEM, TEM and IFM sub-layers for more effective information transformation.
Applying the analysis methods to other sequence-to-sequence tasks like summarization and grammar error correction.
Exploring other architectures such as RNMT, ConvS2S, or document-level NMT.
papers.abstract: There have been significant efforts to interpret the encoder of Transformer-based encoderdecoder architectures for neural machine translation (NMT); meanwhile, the decoder remains largely unexamined despite its critical role. During translation, the decoder must predict output tokens by considering both the source-language text from the encoder and the target-language prefix produced in previous steps. In this work, we study how Transformerbased decoders leverage information from the source and target languages -developing a universal probe task to assess how information is propagated through each module of each decoder layer. We perform extensive experiments on three major translation datasets (WMT En-De, En-Fr, and En-Zh). Our analysis provides insight on when and where decoders leverage different sources. Based on these insights, we demonstrate that the residual feed-forward module in each Transformer decoder layer can be dropped with minimal loss of performance -a significant reduction in computation and number of parameters, and consequently a significant boost to both training and inference speed.

papers.title: Eliciting Chain-of-Thought in Base LLMs via Gradient-Based Representation Optimization
papers.research_question: Can we solely manipulate the hidden states to elicit CoT reasoning from a base LLM, without distorting its language quality?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a gradient-based hidden state optimization method to elicit Chain-of-Thought reasoning in base LLMs, using a balanced likelihood and prior regularization framework to guide hidden states toward reasoning while preserving language quality.
papers.conclusion: Presents a principled gradient-based activation optimization method to elicit CoT reasoning from base LLMs, grounded in probabilistic generation theory, which balances likelihood and prior terms to activate reasoning without distribution shift, and consistently outperforms vector arithmetic methods.
papers.key_findings:
Our method consistently outperforms existing hidden state steering methods across diverse reasoning benchmarks.
The method unlocks latent reasoning capabilities in base LLMs without additional training.
The optimization framework balances reasoning effectiveness and linguistic fluency.
The method is effective across multiple LLM architectures (Mistral, Gemma, Qwen, Phi).
The method's performance depends on the choice of hidden states and layers, with middle layers showing better classification performance.
papers.limitation:
The method can only unlock intrinsic reasoning abilities and cannot inject new capabilities; for models with limited intrinsic reasoning capacity, it cannot create non-existent capabilities.
The method's effectiveness depends on the classification performance and layer selection; improper choices may lead to suboptimal results.
future_direction: Integrating the method with post-training techniques to further amplify reasoning capabilities.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning is a critical capability for large language models (LLMs), enabling them to tackle com- plex multi-step tasks. While base LLMs, pre-trained on general text corpora, often struggle with reasoning due to a lack of specialized training, recent studies reveal their latent reason- ing potential tied to hidden states. However, existing hidden state manipulation methods, such as linear activation steering, suffer from limitations due to their rigid and unconstrained nature, often leading to distribution shifts and degraded text quality. In this work, we propose a novel approach for elic- iting CoT reasoning from base LLMs through hidden state manipulation grounded in probabilistic conditional generation. By reformulating the challenge as an optimization problem with a balanced likelihood and prior regularization framework, our method guides hidden states toward reasoning-oriented trajectories while preserving linguistic coherence. Extensive evaluations across mathematical, commonsense, and logical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our approach con- sistently outperforms existing steering methods, offering a theoretically principled and effective solution for enhancing reasoning capabilities in base LLMs.

papers.title: Converging to a Lingua Franca: Evolution of Linguistic Regions and Semantics Alignment in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do multilingual large language models internally achieve cross-lingual skill transfer through neuron activation patterns and semantic alignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual LLMs develop a common semantic latent space ('Lingua Franca') for processing inputs across languages, with alignment improving through training and scaling.
papers.conclusion: The findings provide insights into the structural evolution of multilingual LLMs during training and scaling, offering a foundation for improving cross-lingual capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron activation patterns are similar for inputs in the same language, revealing key linguistic regions that can be identified and deactivated to impair language-specific performance.
Activation patterns are similar for semantically identical sentences in different languages, indicating mapping to a common semantic space ('Lingua Franca').
With training, key linguistic regions become smaller and activation patterns become more language-agnostic.
Semantic alignment strengthens with training and increased model size, enhancing cross-lingual reasoning ability.
Key neurons are concentrated in the first and last layers, becoming denser in the first layers as training progresses.
papers.limitation:
Analysis primarily focuses on BLOOM and LLaMA2 models, may not generalize to other architectures.
Reliance on specific datasets like Bible and XL-Sum, which may not cover all linguistic nuances.
Methodology based on averaged activation patterns and z-scores may not capture all neuron interactions.
Underlying reasons for patterns remain speculative, requiring further research for causal relationships.
future_direction: Examine a broader range of multilingual LLM architectures.
Utilize more diverse datasets, including low-resource languages.
Apply more sophisticated techniques like causal inference methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, particularly in multilingual contexts. While recent studies suggest that LLMs can transfer skills learned in one language to others, the internal mechanisms behind this ability remain unclear. We observed that the neuron activation patterns of LLMs exhibit similarities when processing the same language, revealing the existence and location of key linguistic regions. Additionally, we found that neuron activation patterns are similar when processing sentences with the same semantic meaning in different languages. This indicates that LLMs map semantically identical inputs from different languages into a "Lingua Franca", a common semantic latent space that allows for consistent processing across languages. This semantic alignment becomes more pronounced with training and increased model size, resulting in a more language-agnostic activation pattern. Moreover, we found that key linguistic neurons are concentrated in the first and last layers of LLMs, becoming denser in the first layers as training progresses. Experiments on BLOOM and LLaMA2 support these findings, highlighting the structural evolution of multilingual LLMs during training and scaling up. This paper provides insights into the internal workings of LLMs, offering a foundation for future improvements in their cross-lingual capabilities.

papers.title: How Chain-of-Thought Works? Tracing Information Flow from Decoding, Projection, and Activation
papers.research_question: How does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting alter a model's internal states to improve reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: CoT works by constraining the decoding space via answer templates, with structural adherence strongly correlating with performance, and modulates neuron activation in a task-dependent manner (reducing activation in open-domain tasks, increasing it in closed-domain tasks).
papers.conclusion: The findings provide a novel mechanistic interpretability framework and critical insights for designing more efficient and robust CoT prompts.
papers.key_findings:
CoT prompts models to imitate structural keywords (e.g., 'time', 'action') from the prompt and content keywords (e.g., numbers) from the input question.
There is a strong positive correlation between adherence to the CoT reasoning structure (measured by Imitation Count) and task performance (accuracy).
CoT leads to more concentrated probability distributions (lower entropy) and higher confidence in generated tokens compared to standard prompting.
CoT reduces the average number of activated neurons in Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) for open-domain tasks, but increases it for closed-domain tasks, indicating task-dependent modulation of neural engagement.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting significantly enhances model reasoning, yet its internal mechanisms remain poorly understood. We analyze CoT's operational principles by reversely tracing information flow across decoding, projection, and activation phases. Our quantitative analysis suggests that CoT may serve as a decoding space pruner, leveraging answer templates to guide output generation, with higher template adherence strongly correlating with improved performance. Furthermore, we surprisingly find that CoT modulates neuron engagement in a task-dependent manner: reducing neuron activation in open-domain tasks, yet increasing it in closed-domain scenarios. These findings offer a novel mechanistic interpretability framework and critical insights for enabling targeted CoT interventions to design more efficient and robust prompts. We released our code and data at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/cot-D247.

papers.title: Large Language Models Are Human-Like Internally
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether surprisal (negative log probability) from internal layers of large language models aligns with human sentence processing data, and whether the alignment varies by layer depth and the type of human measure (behavioral vs. neurophysiological).
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that surprisal from internal layers of larger language models aligns well with human sentence processing data, challenging prior conclusions that focused on final layers. Additionally, it finds that earlier layers align with fast human measures (e.g., gaze duration) and later layers with slower measures (e.g., N400).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that larger language models are cognitively plausible when internal layers are considered, and that different layers correspond to different stages of human sentence processing, advocating for layer-wise alignment in cognitive modeling.
papers.key_findings:
Surprisal from internal layers of larger LMs aligns with human sentence processing data as well as or better than smaller LMs.
The last layer does not yield the best alignment; the best layer varies by human measure.
Earlier layers align better with fast human measures (e.g., first-pass gaze duration, self-paced reading time), while later layers align better with slower measures (e.g., N400, MAZE processing time).
When considering the best internal layer, larger LMs show a positive scaling effect (larger models have higher ∆LL) for most human measures.
The alignment patterns are consistent across multiple languages (tested on MECO corpus).
papers.limitation: The study is focused on naturalistic reading corpora and does not include controlled experiments on syntactic ambiguity or grammatical violation, which are known challenges for surprisal theory.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other probability-based measures such as entropy and entropy reduction.
Combine the internal layer approach with linguistically-motivated neural models.
papers.abstract: Recent cognitive modeling studies have reported that larger language models (LMs) exhibit a poorer fit to human reading behavior (Oh and Schuler, 2023b; Shain et al., 2024; Kuribayashi et al., 2024), leading to claims of their cognitive implausibility. In this paper, we revisit this argument through the lens of mechanistic interpretability and argue that prior conclusions were skewed by an exclusive focus on the final layers of LMs. Our analysis reveals that next-word probabilities derived from internal layers of larger LMs align with human sentence processing data as well as, or better than, those from smaller LMs. This alignment holds consistently across behavioral (self-paced reading times, gaze durations, MAZE task processing times) and neurophysiological (N400 brain potentials) measures, challenging earlier mixed results and suggesting that the cognitive plausibility of larger LMs has been underestimated. Furthermore, we first identify an intriguing relationship between LM layers and human measures: earlier layers correspond more closely with fast gaze durations, while later layers better align with relatively slower signals such as N400 potentials and MAZE processing times. Our work opens new avenues for interdisciplinary research at the intersection of mechanistic interpretability and cognitive modeling.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: Explainable Chain-of-Thought Reasoning: An Empirical Analysis on State-Aware Reasoning Dynamics
papers.research_question: How can we abstract and model the latent structure of chain-of-thought reasoning to provide a global, explainable view of reasoning dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a state-aware transition framework that abstracts chain-of-thought reasoning trajectories into structured latent dynamics via spectral analysis and Markov chains, enabling a global, explainable view of reasoning steps and transitions.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a global perspective on multi-step reasoning in LLMs, uncovering consistent latent structures across models and tasks, and enables explainability applications for CoT reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully abstracts CoT reasoning steps into semantically coherent latent states via spectral embeddings and clustering.
Learned transition patterns are consistent across models and tasks, indicating structured reasoning dynamics beyond surface token sequences.
The latent states correspond to meaningful functional roles (e.g., scenario description, problem framing, answer synthesis).
The Markov chain model captures coherent temporal reasoning flows, validated by Monte Carlo simulations.
The approach enables explainability applications such as semantic role identification and temporal pattern visualization.
papers.limitation:
The framework assumes access to internal representations of open-source language models.
It focuses primarily on intrinsic structural analysis.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting have enabled large language models (LLMs) to perform multi-step reasoning. However, the explainability of such reasoning remains limited, with prior work primarily focusing on local token-level attribution, such that the high-level semantic roles of reasoning steps and their transitions remain underexplored. In this paper, we introduce a state-aware transition framework that abstracts CoT trajectories into structured latent dynamics. Specifically, to capture the evolving semantics of CoT reasoning, each reasoning step is represented via spectral analysis of token-level embeddings and clustered into semantically coherent latent states. To characterize the global structure of reasoning, we model their progression as a Markov chain, yielding a structured and interpretable view of the reasoning process. This abstraction supports a range of analyses, including semantic role identification, temporal pattern visualization, and consistency evaluation.

papers.title: Decoupling Knowledge and Reasoning in LLMs: An Exploration Using Cognitive Dual-System Theory
papers.research_question: How can the contributions of knowledge retrieval and reasoning adjustment be separated and quantified in large language models during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a cognition attribution framework based on dual-system theory to decouple knowledge and reasoning in LLMs, revealing domain-specific reasoning benefits, scaling effects, and a hierarchical separation of knowledge (lower layers) and reasoning (higher layers).
papers.conclusion: The proposed cognition attribution architecture offers a novel perspective for understanding LLM cognition and provides insights into scaling laws, hierarchical knowledge editing, and the reasoning limitations of small models.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning adjustment is domain-specific, benefiting reasoning-intensive domains (e.g., mathematics, physics, chemistry) and potentially impairing knowledge-intensive domains.
Parameter scaling improves both knowledge and reasoning, with knowledge improvements being more pronounced. Scaling also makes reasoning significantly more prudent (reduces overthinking) and modestly more intelligent (increases correction) in specific domains.
Knowledge retrieval primarily occurs in lower network layers, while reasoning adjustments are localized in higher layers, suggesting a functional separation.
Small LLMs tend to overthink more than they correct during reasoning, leading to negative or limited reasoning gains.
LLMs exhibit a human-like anchoring effect, which reasoning adjustment helps to mitigate.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to multiple-choice QA; future work should extend to open-ended generation.
The study does not include ultra-large models (>100B parameters).
The methods are simplified and may not fully capture the underlying mechanisms in LLMs.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to open-ended generation tasks.
Include ultra-large models (>100B parameters) in the study.
Conduct a more in-depth exploration of the phenomena observed using the framework.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) leverage both knowledge and reasoning during inference, the capacity to distinguish between them plays a pivotal role in model analysis, interpretability, and development. Inspired by dual-system cognitive theory, we propose a cognition attribution framework to decouple the contribution of knowledge and reasoning. In particular, the cognition of LLMs is decomposed into two distinct yet complementary phases: knowledge retrieval (Phase 1) and reasoning adjustment (Phase 2). To separate these phases, LLMs are prompted to generate answers under two different cognitive modes, fast thinking and slow thinking, respectively. The performance under different cognitive modes is analyzed to quantify the contribution of knowledge and reasoning. This architecture is employed to 15 LLMs across 3 datasets. Results reveal: (1) reasoning adjustment is domain-specific, benefiting reasoning-intensive domains (e.g., mathematics, physics, and chemistry) and potentially imparing knowledge-intensive domains. (2) Parameter scaling improves both knowledge and reasoning, with knowledge improvements being more pronounced. Additionally, parameter scaling make LLMs reasoning significantly more prudent, while moderately more intelligent. (3) Knowledge primarily resides in lower network layers, while reasoning operates in higher layers. Our framework not only helps understand LLMs from a "decoupling" perspective, but also provides new insights into existing research, including scaling laws, hierarchical knowledge editing, and limitations of small-model reasoning.

papers.title: The Kinetics of Reasoning: How Chain-of-Thought Shapes Learning in Transformers?
papers.research_question: How does chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision affect the learning dynamics and generalization of transformers on formal reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: CoT supervision accelerates generalization in transformers on certain reasoning tasks and can be modeled by a kinetic framework, but it also reveals a transient phase of unfaithfulness where answers are correct but reasoning traces are not.
papers.conclusion: CoT supervision advances the take-off point and often raises the ceiling of generalization, but it also reveals a transient faithfulness gap. Mechanistic analyses show that CoT shifts computation from late, serial pipelines toward earlier, more distributed representations.
papers.key_findings:
CoT generally improves task performance but its benefits depend on task complexity.
CoT accelerates generalization but does not overcome tasks with higher algorithmic complexity, such as finding list intersections.
There is a transient trace unfaithfulness phase where models produce correct answers while skipping or contradicting CoT steps.
CoT alters internal transformer computation mechanistically, shifting computation from late, serial pipelines toward earlier, more distributed representations.
Learning curves for both CoT and non-CoT training can be described by a predictable logistic function in log training steps.
papers.limitation:
The synthetic reasoning tasks used are different from real-world reasoning tasks, and the setup does not assess how natural language understanding (i.e., large-scale pretraining) affects CoT reasoning.
The study uses a fixed-size transformer architecture; extending the study to different model sizes could provide more insights on whether model scale affects the learning dynamics.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision can substantially improve transformer performance, yet the mechanisms by which models learn to follow and benefit from CoT remain poorly understood. We investigate these learning dynamics through the lens of grokking by pretraining transformers on symbolic reasoning tasks with tunable algorithmic complexity and controllable data composition to study their generalization. Models were trained under two settings: (i) producing only final answers, and (ii) emitting explicit CoT traces before answering. Our results show that while CoT generally improves task performance, its benefits depend on task complexity. To quantify these effects, we model the accuracy of the logarithmic training steps with a three-parameter logistic curve, revealing how the learning speed and shape vary with task complexity, data distribution, and the presence of CoT supervision. We also uncover a transient trace unfaithfulness phase: early in training, models often produce correct answers while skipping or contradicting CoT steps, before later aligning their reasoning traces with answers. Empirically, we (1) demonstrate that CoT accelerates generalization but does not overcome tasks with higher algorithmic complexity, such as finding list intersections; (2) introduce a kinetic modeling framework for understanding transformer learning; (3) characterize trace faithfulness as a dynamic property that emerges over training; and (4) show CoT alters internal transformer computation mechanistically.

papers.title: What Happened in LLMs Layers when Trained for Fast vs. Slow Thinking: A Gradient Perspective
papers.research_question: How do fast vs. slow thinking (CoT) affect the layer-wise gradients during LLM training, and what do these gradients reveal about training stability and response correctness?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes layer-wise gradients in LLMs during training and shows that slow thinking (detailed CoT) leads to more stable gradients and helps distinguish correct from irrelevant responses, while fast thinking does not.
papers.conclusion: Our study strengthens fundamental understandings of LLM training and sheds novel insights on its efficiency and stability, which pave the way towards building a generalizable System-2 agent.
papers.key_findings:
Training LLMs for slow thinking (Detailed CoT) leads to similar gradient norms across layers, while fast thinking results in larger gradients in earlier layers and drastic differences across layers.
The gradient of slow thinking helps distinguish correct responses from irrelevant responses. Without CoT, the gradient patterns of the two types of responses are similar.
The instruction-finetuned LLMs do not show superior capability over pre-trained base LLMs in identifying incorrect reasoning paths.
The observations on reasoning tasks cannot be extended to knowledge learning tasks, where simply increasing response length does not show similar gradient patterns as slow thinking.
papers.abstract: What makes a difference in the post-training of LLMs? We investigate the training patterns of different layers in large language models (LLMs) through the lens of the gradient. We are specifically interested in how fast vs. slow thinking affects the layer-wise gradients, given the recent popularity of training LLMs on reasoning paths such as chain-of-thoughts (CoT) and process rewards. In our study, fast thinking without CoT leads to larger gradients and larger differences of gradients across layers than slow thinking (Detailed CoT), indicating the learning stability brought by the latter. Additionally, we study whether the gradient patterns can reflect the correctness of responses when training different LLMs using slow vs. fast thinking paths. The results show that the gradients of slow thinking can distinguish correct and irrelevant reasoning paths. As a comparison, we conduct similar gradient analyses on non-reasoning knowledge learning tasks, on which, however, trivially increasing the response length does not lead to similar behaviors of slow thinking. Our study strengthens fundamental understandings of LLM training and sheds novel insights on its efficiency and stability, which pave the way towards building a generalizable System-2 agent. Our code, data, and gradient statistics can be found in: https://github.com/MingLiiii/Layer_Gradient.

papers.title: Visual Thoughts: A Unified Perspective of Understanding Multimodal Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: Is there a unified explanation for why different multimodal chain-of-thought paradigms enhance large vision-language models in distinct ways?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning improves large vision-language models by incorporating visual thoughts, which act as an intermediate cache for visual information, enabling more efficient and effective reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Visual thoughts provide a unified perspective for understanding how multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning enhances large vision-language models, acting as visual caches that improve information flow and reasoning performance.
papers.key_findings:
Removing visual thoughts from the reasoning process impairs model performance more than reasoning directly from the query alone.
Different expressions of visual thoughts (natural language, structured language, edited image, generative image) vary in effectiveness depending on task clarity and conciseness.
Visual thoughts serve as primary intermediaries, connecting input images to deeper transformer layers and facilitating advanced visual information processing.
Image-form visual thoughts consistently outperform text-form visual thoughts, especially in complex scenarios requiring detailed visual information.
Visual thoughts are more effective than simple image captions for conveying visual information in complex scenes, improving reasoning accuracy.
future_direction: Exploring the integration of multiple visual thoughts to enhance visual information transmission in multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved significant success in multimodal tasks, with multimodal chain-of-thought (MCoT) further enhancing performance and interpretability. Recent MCoT methods fall into two categories: (i) Textual-MCoT (T-MCoT), which takes multimodal input and produces textual output; and (ii) Interleaved-MCoT (I-MCoT), which generates interleaved image-text outputs. Despite advances in both approaches, the mechanisms driving these improvements are not fully understood. To fill this gap, we first reveal that MCoT boosts LVLMs by incorporating visual thoughts, which convey image information to the reasoning process regardless of the MCoT format, depending only on clarity and conciseness of expression.
